acv.quote: We proposed six hundred K a year.

header.tag_why: The store side decided it: the questions moved to stores, then came the workshop requested by Angela's team and the 'partner' install answer, with no live till return and no rollout plan; Angela signed with Adyen, whose pitch was 'one platform for the tills and the website, on one contract' delivered by people who had done store rollouts.

evidence.excerpt: The store couldn't see the online order, so staff were refunding to gift cards or telling people to mail it back.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: they'd just launched a loyalty program that was supposed to work everywhere and didn't, because store and web were two different customer records.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Their COO, Angela, apparently stood in a store on December 27th watching the returns queue.
evidence.label: opinion

trigger.insight: The pain started in the stores, at the returns counter and in the failed loyalty launch, and not at web checkout. The origin story the customer tells is about the COO standing in a store. So the evaluation belonged to operations from day one, even though we sold it as a web and payments deal.
trigger.messaging: Lead retail pitches with the cross-channel return and the single customer record (online order refunded at the till, loyalty that works everywhere), not with checkout conversion.

evidence.excerpt: He ran the RFP, he was my contact the whole way.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Angela.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Probably Angela. Raj wanted us. I think. He told me he did.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Once. The kickoff.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: Tom named the RFP owner as the decider. The person who signed was the COO, and he met her once, at kickoff. Her team asked for the store workshop and she asked for the reference call, so the decisive asks came from someone we never worked. Raj's support is only reported by Raj, and it did not carry the deal.
decider.messaging: In retail deals, build a COO and store-ops track with its own proof points (store rollout, till returns, single accountability), separate from the CTO and web track.

evidence.excerpt: He said they came in with a retail team, people who'd done store rollouts, and they talked about one platform for the tills and the website, on one contract.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And they named retailers Angela knew.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Before, it was all web. Conversion, checkout, wallets. After, it was stores.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Raj forwarded me a list of 14 questions and 11 of them were about stores.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: Everything we know about the competitor comes from Raj after the fact. Even so, the effect is visible: once Adyen showed up with store-rollout people and references the COO recognized, the customer's questions shifted almost entirely to stores (wifi drops, 120-store rollout, Saturday till outages). Adyen changed the evaluation criteria, and we kept answering the old ones.
competitor.messaging: Treat a shift in buyer questions toward stores as a trigger to field store-operations experts and named retail references, not more product slides.

evidence.excerpt: Reaction: the online checkout demo. Their ecommerce lead loved it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence: the unified commerce part.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: that's a diagram.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Then she asked how a return works. Step by step. At the till.
evidence.label: fact

message.insight: M3 failed with exactly the audience it is written for. The head of store operations called it a diagram and immediately asked for the operational reality. The only enthusiasm came from the ecommerce lead, who was not the person signing. Tom's answer to her request was 'I described it', which repeated the diagram problem in words.
message.messaging: Replace M3's abstract claim ('the line between them has pretty much disappeared') with a demonstrable step-by-step till return of an online order, shown live.

evidence.excerpt: When Bev asked who does the installs, I said we'd bring in a partner. She wrote something down and didn't ask another question.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Nobody on our side had run a store rollout.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Right before that, honestly, we were ahead. Raj said so.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I knew on the drive home.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: The turn was the store ops workshop: six store-operations people against our AE and SE, and nobody on our side with rollout experience. The answer 'we'd bring in a partner' collided head-on with Angela's 'I don't want two vendors pointing at each other.' Being 'ahead' according to Raj meant ahead on the web evaluation, which was not where this was decided.
decided.messaging: State plainly who owns installs and store rollout end to end, and give the customer one accountable party; never let 'a partner' be the answer to who shows up.

evidence.excerpt: can I talk to them?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: we couldn't set up a call in time.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Then a rollout plan. Dates, who installs, what happens to the old tills.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: They wanted to watch an online order get returned at a store till, live. We described it. We never showed it.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: All three gaps are about proof, not slides: a peer she could call, a dated rollout plan, and a live till return. A case study (M8) was not enough for a COO who wanted to talk to a peer, while Adyen named retailers she already knew. The live return demo was the single most direct test of the trigger pain, and we never ran it.
gaps.messaging: Back M8 with callable retail references ready on short notice and a standard store rollout plan template (dates, installs, old-till decommissioning), and add a live till-return demo to the retail kit.

evidence.excerpt: 'One system for the tills and the website.' That was Bev, every time.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Angela said, 'I don't want two vendors pointing at each other.'
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: And 'one customer, one basket.'
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: They said 'the tills.'
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: The customer talked about tills, one system, one customer, and one accountable vendor. We talked about 'unified commerce', 'in-person payments' and 'point of sale'. Angela's line about two vendors is about accountability, not technology, and our partner-install answer gave her exactly the two-vendor picture she was trying to avoid.
language.messaging: Rewrite the retail version of M3 in the buyer's words, along the lines of 'one system for the tills and the website, one customer, one basket, one team accountable', and drop the category jargon.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom (and, if possible, Raj) what role Angela played between kickoff and signature, and whether Raj's recommendation was ever put to her.

gaps.question: What did the customer bring up about the competitor?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Raj, or Bev if reachable, what specifically in Adyen's store session convinced them, and which retailers Adyen named.

gaps.question: What did you say when Bev asked how a return works at the till?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and the SE exactly what they described, and why a live till-return demo was not possible before the decision.

gaps.question: Was price or contract structure compared between us and Adyen?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom whether Raj or Angela ever discussed Adyen's commercial terms or how they compared with our six hundred K proposal.

gaps.question: Why couldn't the reference call be set up in time?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and the customer-marketing team what blocked the call with the fashion retailer, and how long it would have taken.

close.rep_takeaway: When a customer's questions shift from web to stores, the decision has moved to a different buyer. Get in front of that person (here the COO, met only once) and bring people who have run store rollouts, a dated rollout plan and a live demo; describing it and offering 'a partner' loses to a competitor who shows up with all three.
